q: Fueling with passengers boarding, on board, or deplaning at the gate is permitted only if certain cabin conditions are met. Name the required states of the Seat Belt Sign and the No Smoking Sign, and one other required condition.
a: The Seat Belt Sign is off and the No Smoking Sign is on. Other required conditions include: all engines shut down, aircraft chocked, a jetbridge/airstairs/boarding ramp at the door, the primary passenger entry door open, electrical power and lights on, and minimum Flight Attendants stationed near a continuously open floor-level exit.

src.quote: Fueling/Defueling/Fuel transferring is permitted while passengers are boarding, remaining on board, or deplaning provided
src.note: The full provided list also requires chocks, all engines shut down, a bridge/stairs/ramp at the door, primary door open, power and lights, Seat Belt Sign off, and No Smoking Sign on.

q: During gate fueling with passengers on board, who is responsible for confirming fueling is complete, and at what point?
a: The Captain verifies fueling is complete prior to door closure.

src.quote: The Captain verifies fueling is complete prior to door closure.
src.note: This is a Captain-specific verification captured in the Note under the at-gate fueling conditions.

q: When fueling with passengers on board away from the gate area (no loading bridge or adequate stairs), what power source and door conditions are required?
a: The APU or GPU must be available, all engines shut down, all doors armed, communications available with the fueler for the duration of fueling, and F/As stationed at their assigned exits keeping the slide deployment areas clear.

src.quote: APU or GPU must be available.
src.note: Communication with the fueler may be by radio, headset, or voice through the First Officer's window, and F/As must be notified when fueling begins and ends.

q: Under what circumstance may an aircraft be fueled with one engine running, and what happens if fleet-specific procedures do not cover it?
a: Fueling with one engine running is only considered where a lack of APU, external power, or ground air would result in a stranded aircraft, per the FH/FCOM procedures. If procedures are not specified in fleet-specific manuals, fueling with one engine running is not authorized.

src.ref: FOM 12.1.1.3 — Fueling with One Engine Running
src.quote: If procedures are not specified in fleet-specific manuals, then fueling with one engine running is not authorized.
src.note: Normally all engines are shut down during fueling; the single-engine-running case is an exception tied to avoiding a stranded aircraft.

q: In a fuel spill with passengers on board, who decides whether to deplane, and on which side of the aircraft are passengers deplaned?
a: The Pilot-In-Command decides whether to deplane (if no pilot is on board, the 'A' Flight Attendant/FFA decides). If there is a choice of exits, passengers are deplaned on the side of the aircraft opposite the fuel spill.

src.quote: passengers will be deplaned on the side of the aircraft opposite the fuel spill.
src.note: Any ground air conditioning unit should also be terminated to prevent pushing fumes into the aircraft and to remove an ignition source.

q: If fueling is required from a non-Alaska Airlines approved fuel vendor, what must be done before fueling begins?
a: Contact Maintenance Control before fueling begins; Maintenance Control provides the Captain with the required fuel acceptance procedures.

src.quote: contact Maintenance Control before fueling begins.
src.note: The Captain does not self-clear a non-approved vendor; Maintenance Control supplies the acceptance procedures.

q: Before operating the aircraft, what are the two acceptable states for every circuit breaker, and how is the 'normal position' identified visually?
a: Every circuit breaker shall be either in the normal position or properly pulled. In the normal position the CB is snapped into the closed position and the white stem is not visible.

src.quote: The CB is snapped into the closed position. The white stem is not visible.
src.note: Company-standard collars for pulled CBs are fluorescent yellow or red, though a different color collar does not affect airworthiness.

q: During a maintenance engine run at the gate, what is the power limit and what flap configuration is required?
a: Engines shall not be operated above idle power at a gate, and flaps shall remain retracted during the maintenance run.

src.ref: FOM 12.3.1 — Maintenance Engine Run at Gate (CAUTION)
src.quote: Engines shall not be operated above idle power at a gate. Flaps shall remain retracted during the maintenance run.
src.note: Pilots are never authorized to conduct high power engine runs for maintenance, defined as any thrust setting above idle.

q: May passengers be on board during a maintenance-run pressurization check, and is fueling permitted during engine runs with passengers aboard?
a: No. Passengers shall not be on board during a pressurization check, and fueling operations during engine runs are prohibited with passengers on board, deplaning, or loading.

src.ref: FOM 12.3.1.1 — Passengers, F/As, and Doors – Passenger Aircraft (WARNING)
src.quote: Passengers shall not be on board during a pressurization check.
src.note: Ramp activity should not be allowed behind an operating engine, and engine runs for an air contamination event or pressurization check are done without passengers/F/As on board.

q: On the 787, what restriction applies to a #1 engine run relative to the boarding door and jetway?
a: #1 engine runs are not permitted with the boarding door(s) open or the jetway extended to the boarding door(s).

src.ref: FOM 12.3.1.2 — Procedure and Safety Requirements – All aircraft
src.quote: #1 engine runs are not permitted with the boarding door(s) open or the jetway extended to the boarding door(s).
src.note: On the 787, doors not used for boarding are also closed to minimize the FOD hazard, both pilots are at their stations, and the aircraft is chocked with the parking brake set.

q: Are pilots ever authorized to conduct high power engine runs for maintenance, and how is 'high power' defined?
a: No. Pilots are not authorized to conduct high power engine runs for maintenance at any time. High power engine runs are defined as any engine thrust setting above idle.

src.ref: FOM 12.3.1.2 — Procedure and Safety Requirements – All aircraft (Note)
src.quote: High power engine runs are defined as any engine thrust setting above idle.
src.note: At the completion of the maintenance idle engine run, the crew completes the Shutdown/Parking Checklist.

q: With a yellow-side MSP-1 displayed on the power/thrust levers, may the aircraft be operated for flight, and what activities are still allowed?
a: No. With the yellow side displayed the aircraft may not be operated for the purpose of flight, but preflight may be performed (including normal Flight Deck flows and checklists, fueling, passenger boarding, etc.). Verbal permission from Maintenance in lieu of the logbook or yellow MSP-1 is not authorized.

src.quote: The aircraft may not be operated for the purpose of flight, but preflight may be performed
src.note: The Flight Crew installs the MSP-1 yellow side out whenever there is an open discrepancy in the logbook.

q: If the MSP-1 card is not installed and the logbook is not in the Flight Deck, how is the aircraft's status treated?
a: The aircraft status is treated as if the card were installed with the RED side up until the logbook is returned to the Flight Deck (i.e., systems/controls cannot be operated by non-Maintenance personnel).

src.quote: the aircraft status will be treated as if the card were installed with the RED side up until the logbook is returned to the Flight Deck.
src.note: The red side warns that safety-sensitive maintenance is being performed and non-Maintenance personnel may not operate systems or controls.

q: If an aircraft is designated Out of Service and the ACARS OTS message is received, what must occur before pushback even if the defect has been signed off?
a: Dispatch must be contacted prior to pushback even if the defect resolution has been signed off and the aircraft has been released.

src.quote: If the ACARS OTS message is received, Dispatch must be contacted prior to pushback even if the defect resolution has been signed off and the aircraft has been released.
src.note: The OTS designation auto-generates an ACARS message to the aircraft and Dispatch when the Load Closeout is sent.

q: For the 787, a high-speed rejected takeoff requires a Maintenance Logbook entry above what speed, and what three items must be noted?
a: Above 80 kts. Note the gross weight, reject speed, and braking effort.

src.quote: (Boeing) 80 kts (note gross weight, reject speed, braking effort)
src.note: This is one of many mandatory logbook entries, alongside limitation exceedances, hard/overweight landings, and returns for landing due to mechanical reasons.

q: For an HA aircraft, on what time reference is the MEL valid period based, and may an aircraft depart with an MEL that will expire during the flight?
a: For HA, the MEL valid period is based on GMT, and an aircraft may not depart a station with an MEL whose time limit will expire during the planned duration of the flight.

src.quote: An aircraft may not depart a station with an MEL whose time limit will expire during the planned duration of the flight.
src.note: By contrast, the AS valid period is based on Seattle local time and a flight may be dispatched if departure is within the valid period even if it ends outside it.

q: For a non-ETOPS HA flight, how long is the Overnight Check valid in flight hours and in clock hours?
a: The Overnight Check is valid for 25 flight hours in service and must not exceed 48 consecutive clock hours. A Post Flight Check does not reset the 48-hour Overnight Check requirement.

src.quote: The Overnight Check is valid for 25 flight hours in service and must not exceed 48 consecutive clock hours.
src.note: The PIC must verify the Airworthiness Release was signed off in the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook prior to each non-ETOPS flight or group of flights.

q: May an aircraft depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook, and what entry must Maintenance make at major maintenance airports for open entries?
a: No aircraft will be allowed to depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook. At major maintenance airports, Maintenance must make a balancing entry in the 'Action Taken' or 'Correction/Deferral' column for all open entries.

src.quote: No aircraft will be allowed to depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook.
src.note: Under the Crew Placarding Procedure the MOC may direct the Flight Crew to complete the balancing entry to return the aircraft to service.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You're the Captain at the gate, passengers boarding, fuel truck pumping. Your new First Officer, wanting to reduce cabin glare, reaches up and turns the No Smoking Sign OFF while leaving the Seat Belt Sign ON, and fueling continues. What is wrong, and what are the correct sign states plus the exit condition you must confirm?
a: The FO has both signs backwards. Fueling with passengers requires SONO: Seat Belt Sign OFF, No Smoking Sign ON. He must reverse both. You must also confirm chocks, all engines shut down, a bridge/stairs/ramp at the door, the primary door open, power and lights, and minimum Flight Attendants stationed near a floor-level exit that remains continuously open as the deplaning route.

src.quote: Fueling/Defueling/Fuel transferring is permitted while passengers are boarding, remaining on board, or deplaning provided
src.note: The provided list requires the Seat Belt Sign off and the No Smoking Sign on (SONO), plus chocks, all engines shut down, a bridge/stairs/ramp at the door, primary door open, power and lights, and an FA at a continuously open floor-level exit.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Maintenance requests a #1 engine idle run at the gate to troubleshoot. The jetway is still extended to the forward boarding door, which is open with two agents aboard. May you start the #1 engine, and what must change first?
a: No. On the 787, #1 engine runs are not permitted with the boarding door(s) open or the jetway extended to the boarding door(s). Retract the jetway and close that door first. Doors not used for boarding are closed to minimize FOD, both pilots must be at their stations, the aircraft chocked with parking brake set, and a dedicated Engine Safety Observer stationed at the side of the engine.

src.ref: FOM 12.3.1.2 — Procedure and Safety Requirements – All aircraft
src.quote: #1 engine runs are not permitted with the boarding door(s) open or the jetway extended to the boarding door(s).
src.note: Doors not used for boarding are closed to minimize the FOD hazard; both pilots at their stations, aircraft chocked, parking brake set, dedicated Engine Safety Observer at the engine.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: At a remote station your APU is MEL'd inoperative, there is no ground power and no ground air, and you'll be stranded if you shut down. Ground crew asks if you can hot-fuel with the #2 engine running. Your 787 manuals publish no procedure for single-engine-running fueling. Are you authorized?
a: No. Fueling with one engine running is only considered where a lack of APU, external power, or ground air would strand the aircraft, and only per the FH/FCOM procedure. Because your 787 fleet-specific manuals do not specify a procedure, fueling with one engine running is not authorized regardless of the stranding risk.

src.ref: FOM 12.1.1.3 — Fueling with One Engine Running
src.quote: If procedures are not specified in fleet-specific manuals, then fueling with one engine running is not authorized.
src.note: Fueling with one engine running is only considered where a lack of APU, external power, or ground air will result in a stranded aircraft, per the FH/FCOM.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: After block-in at an outstation with no HA maintenance, you write up a discrepancy. Maintenance Control says the item is deferrable and directs you via ACARS to make a balancing entry to return the aircraft to service. The outbound Captain sees an open write-up with nothing in the 'Action Taken/Correction/Deferral' column. May the aircraft depart as-is, and who may direct the balancing entry?
a: No aircraft may depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook. At major maintenance airports Maintenance makes the balancing entry in the 'Action Taken' or 'Correction/Deferral' column for all open entries. When authorized under the Crew Placarding Procedure, the MOC may direct the Flight Crew to complete that column to return the aircraft to service.

src.quote: No aircraft will be allowed to depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook.
src.note: At major maintenance airports Maintenance makes a balancing entry in the Action Taken or Correction/Deferral column; under the Crew Placarding Procedure the MOC may direct the Flight Crew to complete it.
